usage: Polite-neutral; the standard way to ask if someone's taken

Same frame, swap to 여자친구 / 여친
Softer, less direct — 'someone you're meeting' rather than a labeled partner

Do you have a boyfriend?
The bare question; rising tone makes it a yes/no

Do you maybe have a boyfriend?
혹시 ('by any chance') cushions a slightly nosy question

The clipped forms 남친/여친 are very common in casual speech and texting, but in a first polite conversation use the full 남자친구/여자친구. A gentler near-synonym is 만나는 사람 있어요? ('are you seeing someone?'), which avoids the committed label and feels less blunt when you barely know the person, or when you're hinting at your own interest. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: many add 를 (남자친구를 있어요?), but 있다 takes the subject particle 이/가 or none at all in speech — never the object 을/를. Also, asking a near-stranger this with no 혹시 or reason can feel intrusive, so soften it. To an older person, raise it to 있으세요?.

What's your ideal type, may I ask?

What's your type?

What's your type? Mine's tall people.

You're totally my type.

english: I fell for you at first sight
usage: I fell for you at first sight
Polite; a sweet confession of instant attraction
I fell for you at first sight
반말, to a partner or crush
I was smitten in an instant
examples: 사실 첫눈에 반했어요.
Honestly, I fell for you at first sight.
사실 ('actually') makes it a soft confession
처음 봤을 때 첫눈에 반했어.
The first time I saw you, I fell for you instantly.
처음 봤을 때 ('when I first saw') sets the scene
그 사람한테 완전 반해서 잠도 안 와요.
I'm so smitten with them I can't even sleep.
반하다 + 한테 ('with'); 잠도 안 와 ('can't sleep')

The core verb 반하다 means to be captivated by someone, and crucially its target takes 에게/한테 ('to/by'), NOT 을/를: 너한테 반했어 ('I fell for YOU'), so the English-speaker's instinct to say 너를 반했어 is wrong. Note 반하다 is almost always used in the PAST (반했어요 'I've fallen for you') because it describes a state you've already entered — saying present 반해요 sounds incomplete. Pitfall: don't confuse 반하다 ('be smitten') with the unrelated 반하다 homophones or with 반갑다 ('glad to meet') — totally different. 반말; the playful question between two people in the gray zone
Are we sort of seeing each other?

Describing the relationship status to a friend

Are you talking to anyone these days?

썸만 타다가 흐지부지됐어요.
We were just in that stage and it fizzled out.

english: Will you go out with me?

반말, once you're close or younger
Let's date / let's be a couple
A statement-style ask, gentle and warm
Earnest, almost confession-like; 주세요 makes it a heartfelt request

Will you go out with me?

나 너 좋아해. 우리 사귈래?
I like you. Want to go out?
Confession (좋아해) then the ask, the standard one-two
우리 오늘부터 1일이에요.
Today's day one for us.
Said the moment you agree to date; couples count from 1일

The receiving side; 받다 ('to receive') flips the direction

Polite; expressing the wish to ask for a date
반말, declaring your intention to a friend/crush
Want to go on a date?
The soft opener that leads into asking someone out

I'd like to ask you out.
A sincere, slightly nervous way to open
우리 이번 주말에 데이트할래요?

'wind arises', meaning an affair has happened / someone has been swept into one) — you say 바람피우지 마 ('don't cheat', commanding behavior) but 바람났대 ('I heard they had an affair', describing the event). usage: Polite; saying a couple looks/fits good together
You two really suit each other
Said about a couple by an onlooker; 진짜 ('really')
You're a match made in heaven
examples: 우리 진짜 잘 어울리는 것 같아.
I think we really go well together.
-는 것 같다 ('I think/seems') softens it sweetly
둘이 너무 잘 어울려요!
You two suit each other so well!
A compliment to a couple; 둘이 ('the two of you')
이 옷 너한테 잘 어울려.
This outfit suits you well.
Same verb for clothing — 'it suits you'
nuance: 어울리다 means 'to match / suit / go well together', and 우리 잘 어울려요 is the warm way to say a couple fits — looks good together, has chemistry. It's also the everyday verb for clothes suiting a person (이 색 잘 어울려요 'this color suits you'), so it spans both 'we're a good couple' and 'that looks good on you'. The key contrast is 어울리다 vs. 사귀다: 어울리다 is about COMPATIBILITY/fit (we match), while 사귀다 is the relationship STATUS (we're dating) — saying 우리 잘 어울려 doesn't mean you're official, just that you'd fit. For destiny-level praise, Koreans escalate to 천생연분 ('heaven-made match') or 잘 맞다 ('we click / are compatible', more about personality fit). usage: 반말; calling out someone's hot-and-cold behavior
Please don't play hard to get
Are you playing hard to get?
Asking, half-amused, if it's a tactic
You're good at the push-pull game
examples: 솔직하게 말해, 밀당하지 마.
Just be honest, don't play games.
솔직하게 ('honestly') contrasts with the game-playing
답장 일부러 늦게 해? 밀당하는 거야?
Are you texting back late on purpose? Playing hard to get?
일부러 ('on purpose') names the tactic
밀당도 적당히 해야지.
You should keep the push-pull in moderation.

nuance: 밀당 is a slangy contraction of 밀고 당기기 ('pushing and pulling'), the dating game of playing hot-and-cold — acting interested then aloof to keep someone hooked. 밀당하다 ('to do push-pull') = to play hard to get / play games. The contrast to draw: 밀당 (strategic push-pull, a tactic) vs. 튕기다 ('to play coy / pretend reluctance', literally 'to bounce', often refusing/holding back at first to seem less eager) — they overlap, but 밀당 is the ongoing back-and-forth strategy, while 튕기다 is more 'feigning reluctance' at a single moment (acting reluctant or hard-to-get when first asked, to seem less eager). english: We've hit a rough patch / lost the spark
usage: We've hit a slump in our relationship
Polite; describing a stale phase in a long relationship
I think we're in a slump
We got through the rough patch
극복하다 ('to overcome') — came out the other side
examples: 요즘 권태기 왔나 봐.
I think we've hit a rough patch lately.
-나 봐 ('seems like') for a soft guess
3년 사귀니까 권태기가 오더라고요.
After dating 3 years, the slump set in.
-더라고요 reports a realized experience
권태기인데 헤어지긴 싫어요.
We're in a slump, but I don't want to break up.
Contrast 권태기 with not wanting to 헤어지다
nuance: 권태기 (Sino-Korean 倦怠期, lit. 'weariness period') is the relationship 'slump' — the stage in a long-term couple when the excitement fades and things feel routine, like the English 'we've lost the spark' or 'the honeymoon's over'. It's collocated with 오다 ('to come'): 권태기가 오다 ('the slump comes/arrives'), as if it's a phase that visits you — a very Korean way to frame emotional states as arriving (cf. 사춘기가 오다 'puberty hits'). The contrast: 권태기 (boredom/staleness in an ongoing relationship) is NOT a breakup — couples talk about 권태기 극복 ('overcoming the slump'); whereas 헤어지다 is actually splitting up. So 권태기 왔어 ≠ 'we broke up'; it means the relationship feels stale. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) the verb — it's 권태기가 오다 (it 'comes'), not 권태기를 하다 or 가지다; learners wrongly try to 'have' it as an object. (2) It implies a fairly established relationship — you wouldn't say 권태기 about a week-old fling. Register: 권태기 is normal everyday vocabulary, fine in polite or casual; 권태기가 왔어요 (polite) works confiding to anyone, 권태기 왔어 with friends.

usage: Polite; the breakup line, said gently but seriously
Softer phrasing — 'stop meeting' instead of the blunt 헤어지다
Reporting the breakup to others, past tense
examples: 미안해. 우리 헤어지자.
I'm sorry. Let's break up.
-자 ('let's') 반말; 미안해 cushions the blow
우리 그만 만나는 게 좋겠어요.
I think we'd better stop seeing each other.
-는 게 좋겠어요 ('it'd be better to') — a gentle, indirect breakup
남자친구랑 헤어졌어요. 너무 힘들어요.
I broke up with my boyfriend. It's so hard.
헤어지다 + 랑 ('with'); 힘들다 ('it's hard')
nuance: 헤어지다 means 'to break up / part', and 우리 헤어져요 is the direct breakup line. Crucially, 헤어지다 is intransitive and reciprocal — it means 'to part (from each other)', so the partner is marked with 와/랑/하고 ('with'), NOT 을/를: 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요 ('I broke up WITH my boyfriend'). The single most common English-speaker error is 남자친구를 헤어졌어요 with the object particle — wrong; you part WITH someone, you don't 'break up someone'. Note 헤어지다 also just means 'to part ways' in a neutral sense (after meeting, 여기서 헤어져요 'let's part here / say bye here'), but in dating context it's the romantic breakup. Softer alternatives Koreans use to avoid the harsh word: 그만 만나다 ('stop seeing each other') and 그만 만나는 게 좋겠어 — gentler than the blunt 헤어지자. english: I want to get back together
usage: I want to get back together
Polite-formal; wanting to reunite with an ex
I want to see you / be together again
반말, warmer and plainer than the formal 재회
A tender invitation to restart the relationship
I got back together with my ex
examples: 헤어졌지만 아직도 재회하고 싶어요.
We broke up, but I still want to get back together.
헤어졌지만 ('though we split') sets up the longing
우리 다시 만날까? 한 번만 더 해보자.
Should we get back together? Let's try just one more time.
다시 만나다 + 한 번만 더 ('just once more')
재회해도 똑같을까 봐 무서워요.
I'm scared it'll be the same even if we reunite.
-ㄹ까 봐 ('afraid that') — fear of repeating
nuance: 재회하다 (Sino-Korean 再會 're-meet' + 하다) means 'to reunite / get back together', the formal-ish word for rekindling with an ex. In everyday speech, though, Koreans more often say the plainer 다시 만나다 ('meet again / get back together') — 재회 sounds a touch literary or like a 'reunion' headline, so 전 남친이랑 다시 만나요 ('I'm seeing my ex again') is the casual norm, while 재회하고 싶어요 is more earnest/formal. Don't confuse 재회 ('reunite, get back together') with 화해 ('to make up / reconcile after a fight') — you 화해 after an argument (still together), but you 재회 after you'd actually broken up.
